title: Exposing our dark secret; Inquest into reserve jail deaths
article: When a drunken Ricardo Wesley, his blood-alcohol level three times the legal limit, somehow lit the foam mattress in his unheated cell in a condemned police station in the isolated First Nations community of Kashechewan, he put the final link in a chain of events that was tragically predictable in the clear vision of 20-20 hindsight.
It killed him, at age 22, and it killed 20-year-old Jamie Goodwin, a second inmate who was locked up one cell away.
The two perished -- screaming for their lives -- as the building burned to the ground, the only firetruck inoperable.

As a coroner's jury heard yesterday -- the inquest being held here instead of far-north Cochrane in order to hopefully give it the oxygen of publicity provided by big-city media -- the jail cells at this Nishnawbe-Aski Police Service (NAPS) detachment on the shores of James Bay had no heat, no running water, no fire extinguisher, no sprinklers, and no universal key system.
The cell doors, in fact, were padlocked, and the keys unnumbered and untagged.
The foam mattress and whatever blankets existed were apparently not fire retardant, nor were prisoners presumably disallowed from smoking.
The place smelled like urine.

Back in August, 2001, federal public works recommended the building be razed, yet it took four years for a modular replacement to land on the reserve and it sat there, still unassembled, on that January day in 2006 when Ricardo Wesley was picked up by police on the reserve, three sheets to the wind, and with the thermometer reading minus 25.
In fact, the replacement has yet to be erected.

The blaze was so intense that forensic toxicologist Teri Martin testified that blood samples taken during Ricardo Wesley's autopsy were so "cooked" that they were useless to measure for blood-alcohol readings, and that urine samples had to be used -- giving Wesley a reading near the time of his death of 246 mg. of alcohol per 100 mg. of blood, or three times the legal limit of 80.

Jamie Goodwin, meanwhile, having been picked up on his snowmachine for suspected impairment three hours before, died with his blood showing it was down to half the legal alcohol limit, but still showing significant traces of marijuana's THC chemical.

According to opening statements by coroner's court lawyer Margaret Creal, five NAPS police officers were on duty the day of the fire but, by the time someone yelled out "Emergency! Emergency!," that final link in the chain of documented events had sealed the inevitable conclusion.

Smoke was already visible. In Ricardo Wesley's cell, a "large object on the floor was on fire." The padlock on the cell was already too hot to touch. The keys were unmarked, and the right key could not be found.
Bolt cutters had to be sought out. There was no water, no fire extinguisher, and no community fire equipment that was not broken.
One officer, Claudius Koosees, had to be rescued when he was found crawling along the floor of the cell area, the back of his jacket on fire.
Wesley and Goodwin, however, were soon engulfed.
The inquest, heard before Dr. David Eden, is expected to last up to five weeks.

And there is no shortage of lawyers -- separate lawyers representing the Wesley and Goodwin families, both in attendance yesterday, plus lawyers representing everyone from NAPS, the Ontario Ministry of Community Safety and Corrections, the federal government, the police officers, the band council to First Nation regional governments -- all adding up to nine separate legal representations.

While the in-custody deaths of Ricardo Wesley and Jamie Goodwin were the mandatory reason for the inquest being called, the focus has already begun to turn to the living conditions on the Kashechewan First Nation reserve.

"My hope is that the recommendations that come from this inquest will help improve the conditions that we live under and help ensure that no one else has to die in the circumstances that my son died under," George Wesley said though a Cree interpreter.
His thoughts were echoed by Kashechewan Chief Jonathan Solomon who, outside the inquest, said "it was about time the truth came out."
"We live in deplorable conditions," he said. "If the story comes out the way the story should come out, maybe it will open some eyes and provoke change."

The Kashechewan community is comprised of approximately 1,700 people. There have been five emergency evacuations between 2005 and 2008 -- four because of flooding and once amid a tainted-water crisis.
No roads lead to Kashechewan.
It is fly-in only.

According to a brief put out by Aboriginal Legal Services of Toronto, this isolated community also suffers from poor health and is plagued by a high rate of suicide, having once reported 21 suicide attempts by youth in one month alone.

It must have been an eye-opener for the five members of the coroner's jury -- three of them women, one of whom is Asian but none visibly aborginal, and all chosen from the Toronto jury pool -- who spent a day up in Kashechewan during March in order to get a lay of the land.

As Julian Falconer, counsel for the Wesley family, put it: "It is my hope that this inquest will expose one of Canada's darkest secrets -- the deplorable conditions on northern First Nation communities."
Only time will tell.
